## Speeding up data handling

::: callout-note
## Reading task: \~4 minutes

Because our app is an example, speed is not really an issue when loading
in data. But imagine you had a large sequencing dataset with thousands
of genes from hundreds of samples - suddenly loading speed (and
performance) can become an issue. If data can be organized as csv files,
this is usually a good option - csv files can be loaded in rapidly using
the `vroom()` function from the package of the same name. But if your
dataset is very large and your app feels clunky, there are a few options
you can utilize

If file size is the issue, consider converting file format to the
parquet format. Parquet is similar to csv but structures data in a
different way. Generally, the form is optimized for machines rather than
humans, as we cannot open and interact with it the way we can with a
csv. But for our apps, this does not matter too much.

You can convert data to parquet using the `arrow` package. If you want
to save our penguin dataset in a folder called "data-raw", you use the
command

```{r}
#| eval: false

#create the data-raw folder

usethis::use_data_raw()

#save our data as parquet
arrow::write_parquet(x = penguins,
                     sink = here::here("data-raw/penguins.parquet"))

```

Then data can be read in using
`arrow::read_parquet("data-raw/penguins.parquet")` If you are interested
in how much more efficient parquet is, this [blog
post](https://motherduck.com/learn/csv-vs-parquet-benchmark/) provides
some indication: for a data set with 11 mio rows, parquet files were
6.8x smaller than csv, and processed 22-60x faster.

If loading is not the issue, but data wrangling is (for example
filtering steps) then an alternative is to use
[duckplyr](https://duckplyr.tidyverse.org/). Duckplyr uses the powerful
duckdb engine to compute results faster. `duckplyr` works as a faster
drop-in for dplyr. If you call `library(duckplyr)` in a normal R script,
`duckplyr` will overwrite dplyr methods. In a shiny app (especially
using golem where we modularize things) it can be a bit more tricky -
you should explicitely call `duckplyr::methods_overwrite()` in the
`run_app.R` script just before `with_golem_options()`. I have not
verified this approach yet - but you should be able to get the speed by
adding `duckplyr::as_duckdb_tibble()` in the top of your data wrangling
steps:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
penguins |> 
  duckplyr::as_duckdb_tibble() |> 
  dplyr::filter(sex == "female")
  
```

These methods work best if you have data that can be stored as a data
frame. For some of our omics data (like single cell RNAseq data) this
can be notoriously difficult, and objects from for example `seurat` can
take a long time to load into R. This makes it difficult to use the
tools above. My best advice here is to delete as much as you can from
the Seurat datasets - they often end up being filled with
normalizations. Consider checking out he package
[DietSeurat](https://rdrr.io/cran/Seurat/man/DietSeurat.html) or setting
aspects of the seurat object (such as count and scale.data) to NULL.
:::

## Making interactive plots

After all this reading, it is time to code some plots. We can start by
making a plot exploring the possible relation between bill length and
flipper length for different species of penguins.But first, let's go in
and delete the golem welcome page:

```{r}
#| eval: false

app_ui <- function(request) {
  tagList(
    # Leave this function for adding external resources
    golem_add_external_resources(),
    # Your application UI logic
    bslib::page_navbar(
      bslib::nav_panel(
        title = "Our awesome penguin app",
        mod_overview_ui("overview_1")
      )

    )
  )
}
```

We first build the UI code:

```{r}
#| eval: false
mod_overview_ui <- function(id) {
  ns <- NS(id)
  tagList(
    bslib::card(
      bslib::card_header("penguin plot"),
      shiny::plotOutput(outputId = "penguinplot")
    )
  )
}

```

Then we need to decide what should be rendered on the server side:

```{r}
#| eval: false

mod_overview_server <- function(id){
  moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session){
    ns <- session$ns
    
    output$penguinplot <- shiny::renderPlot({
      ggplot2::ggplot(
        penguins,
        ggplot2::aes(
          x = bill_len,
          y = flipper_len,
          color = species
        )
      )+
        ggplot2::geom_point()+
        ggplot2::theme_bw()
    })
  })
}

```

This should modify our app to render a plot like the following

```{r}
      ggplot2::ggplot(
        penguins,
        ggplot2::aes(
          x = bill_len,
          y = flipper_len,
          color = species
        )
      )+
        ggplot2::geom_point()+
        ggplot2::theme_bw()
    
```

But surprisingly it does not work! Our app is just blank? Where is our
beautiful plot? To render it properly, we need to add a small wrapper to
our outputId. It should be changed from `outputId = "penguinplot"` to
`outputId = ns("penguinplot)"`. You may notice our server code contains
a reference to ns in the line `ns <- session$ns`. What this does is
essentially a way for our modularized app to navigate where input and
output id's belong in our various modules. Always add `ns("")` around
input and output IDs!

```{r}
#| eval: false
mod_overview_ui <- function(id) {
  ns <- NS(id)
  tagList(
    bslib::card(
      bslib::card_header("penguin plot"),
      shiny::plotOutput(outputId = ns("penguinplot"))
    )
  )
}

```

If we now run `golem::run_dev()` we see our plot. But right now it is
static. What if we wanted to make it more interactive? There is a
powerful alternative to ggplot called `plotly`. In this package
interactivity is native. But the syntaxt of plotly is different. The
equivalent of the above would be

```{r}
#| message: false

plotly::plot_ly(
  data = penguins,
  x =~bill_len,
  y = ~flipper_len,
  color = ~species,
  type = "scatter" 
)

```

We see here there are several nice functionalities - we can zoom, we can
export and there is a native tooltip - if we hover above individual
points, we can get info about them. We can customise the content of
these, but it requires some finesse. Luckily there is a way we can
convert our ggplot to plotly easily, using the `ggplotly` function.

```{r}
penguin_plotly <- ggplot2::ggplot(
        penguins,
        ggplot2::aes(
          x = bill_len,
          y = flipper_len,
          color = species
        )
      )+
        ggplot2::geom_point()+
        ggplot2::theme_bw()

plotly::ggplotly(penguin_plotly)
```

We can customize tooltip information in `ggplotly`. We can for example
add information about the sex of the penguin by adding it as a text info
in ggplot, and call it in `gglotly`:

```{r}
penguin_plotly <- ggplot2::ggplot(
        penguins,
        ggplot2::aes(
          x = bill_len,
          y = flipper_len,
          color = species
        )
      )+
        ggplot2::geom_point(
          ggplot2::aes(
            text = sex
          )
        )+
        ggplot2::theme_bw()

plotly::ggplotly(penguin_plotly,
                 tooltip = "text")
```

Before we try to run it in our app, we have one important thing to do in
the UI - we must change our
`shiny::plotOutput(outputId = ns("penguinplot"))` to
`plotly::plotlyOutput(outputId = ns("penguinplot"))` and likewise change

`output$penguinplot <- shiny::renderPlot({` to
`output$penguinplot <- plotly::renderPlotly({`

Once this is done, we should be good to go.

## Filtering and subsetting

So far, most of what we have done could be achieved in a static
document. But shiny offers a lot more - particularly the ability to
respond to our inputs. Lets take our plot above - say we want the
ability to filter our plot based on what island the penguins are from.

```{r}
penguins |> 
  dplyr::distinct(island)
```

We see we have three options - Torgersen, Biscoe and Dream. We can make
an `input` containing these three options in our ui, plus a fourth
containing all of them.

```{r}
#| eval: false

mod_overview_ui <- function(id) {
  ns <- NS(id)
  tagList(
    bslib::card(
      bslib::card_header("penguin plot"),
      shiny::radioButtons(inputId = ns("island"),
                          label = "Select island",
                          choices = c("all",
                                      "Torgersen",
                                      "Biscoe",
                                      "Dream"),
                          selected = "all"),
      plotly::plotlyOutput(outputId = ns("penguinplot"))
    )
  )
}
```

If we run `golem::run_dev()` we will now see a radiobutton with four
choices. But they don't do anything yet. To link the choice to our plot,
we must modify the code for our plot. If we just want to filter the data
set based on which island has been chosen, we need the name of our
`input` - in this case "island". we could just do something like the
following:

```{r}
#| eval: false

penguin_subset <- penguins |> 
  dplyr::filter(island == input$island)

penguin_plotly <- ggplot2::ggplot(
        penguin_subset,
        ggplot2::aes(
          x = bill_len,
          y = flipper_len,
          color = species
        )
      )+
        ggplot2::geom_point(
          ggplot2::aes(
            text = sex
          )
        )+
        ggplot2::theme_bw()

plotly::ggplotly(penguin_plotly,
                 tooltip = "text")

```

This will work for chosing the island, but how about if we want the
option to show the whole dataset? We can do it with an if/else
statement. If we have selected "all" we use the entire penguins
dataset - else we will filter for the content of input\$island. In R
code it looks like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false

if(input$island == "all"){
  penguin_subset <- penguins
}
else {
  penguin_subset <- penguins |> 
  dplyr::filter(island == input$island)
}

penguin_plotly <- ggplot2::ggplot(
        penguin_subset,
        ggplot2::aes(
          x = bill_len,
          y = flipper_len,
          color = species
        )
      )+
        ggplot2::geom_point(
          ggplot2::aes(
            text = sex
          )
        )+
        ggplot2::theme_bw()

plotly::ggplotly(penguin_plotly,
                 tooltip = "text")
```

We can now change our plot based on input! This is just one example of
reactivity in shiny. There are many ways to change input - for a gallery
check [this
resource](https://shiny.posit.co/r/gallery/widgets/widget-gallery/)

## :technologist: Exercise: observeEvent

**Time: \~6 minutes.**

Another helpful function to know is `shiny::observeEvent()`. this
function is coded into the server part and when the condition is
triggered, the code is run. Try this out by adding the following:

1.  In the UI, add an action button
    `shiny::actionButton(inputId = ns("test")`.
2.  In the server add

```{r}
#| echo: false

shiny::observeEvent(input$test,{
    print("testing!") 
  })
```

3.  Run the app, press the button and watch the console for the output

scheme. Or try adding a different module with a different plot.

## Summary

- We have now learned how to speed up loading and performance of our app
- We also know how to make plots interactive
- Finally we have learned how to make Shiny responsive and change the
  output based on our input.
